title: ISC Inquiry From Corporations Canada: How to Respond
h1: An ISC Inquiry From Corporations Canada: What It Means and How to Respond in 30 Days
description: Received an ISC inquiry email from Corporations Canada? You have 30 days to respond. What the notice means, how to reply, and how to fix your ISC register.
body:
**Got an ISC inquiry from Corporations Canada?** You have 30 days from the date on the notice to respond. [File your federal annual return with updated ISC information →](/order/annual-return?src=article-corporations-canada-isc-inquiry) — {{price:annual-return}} all-in + tax, filed within 1 business day.

An ISC inquiry is an official email from Corporations Canada asking your federal (CBCA) corporation to prove its individuals with significant control (ISC) filing is accurate — and it gives you **30 days from the date of the notice** to respond. Starting in the fall of 2026, Corporations Canada began emailing these inquiries to corporations that have filed annual returns, particularly those that reported having *no* individuals with significant control. The inquiry is not an accusation and not a penalty — but ignoring it can put your corporation in default, with consequences that run from a refused Certificate of Compliance up to steps toward administrative dissolution. This guide covers what the email means, exactly how to respond within the deadline, and how to set up your ISC register so you never get another one.

## What is an ISC inquiry from Corporations Canada?

It's a compliance check on your beneficial-ownership filing. Since January 22, 2024, every CBCA corporation (apart from a handful of exclusions, such as reporting issuers and Crown corporations) must file information about its individuals with significant control with Corporations Canada — at incorporation, with every annual return, and within 15 days of recording any change in its ISC register. Part of that information, including each ISC's full legal name and a description of how they hold control, is [publicly searchable](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/corporations-canada/en/individuals-significant-control/individuals-significant-control-file-your-information) on the federal corporation database.

An ISC is, broadly, an individual who owns or controls **25% or more** of the corporation's voting shares, **25% or more** of its shares by fair market value, or who has "control in fact" over the corporation — directly, indirectly, or jointly with others. (Our [guide to Canada's corporate transparency registers](/articles/corporate-transparency-registers-canada) covers the full rules, province by province.)

The inquiry campaign, reported by national law firms in September 2026, is Corporations Canada checking that those filings are real. The email asks the corporation to confirm it took appropriate steps to identify its ISCs and that what it filed is properly supported. Receiving one doesn't mean you did anything wrong — but the 30-day response window is stated on the notice, and the clock starts on the notice date, not the day you open the email.

One caution before anything else: the inquiry comes by email, and so do phishing attempts dressed up as government notices. Before acting, verify the sender is a legitimate Corporations Canada address and that any link points to ised-isde.canada.ca or canada.ca — or skip the links entirely and respond through the [Online Filing Centre](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/corporations-canada/en/individuals-significant-control/individuals-significant-control-file-your-information) you already use for annual returns.

## Why did your corporation get one?

The pattern reported so far: corporations that filed **"no ISC"** declarations are the most likely targets. When a corporation can't identify any ISCs — or determines none exist — its register must contain a statement to that effect *plus a summary of the steps it took* to reach that conclusion. Many corporations ticked the "none" option without documenting any steps, and those filings are exactly what the inquiries probe.

"No ISC" filings are legitimately common — for example, where four or more unrelated shareholders each hold under 25% and nobody has control in fact. But they're also the filing a corporation makes when the real owners are buried behind holding companies, trusts, or nominees, which is why they draw scrutiny. If your corporation sits inside a holding-company structure, remember the register must look through the corporate layers to the *individuals* at the top of the chain: a corporation owned 100% by a holdco almost always has an ISC — the person who controls the holdco.

Other filings can draw an inquiry too: registers that never change year over year, filings that conflict with other records, or a discrepancy reported to Corporations Canada. Since October 1, 2025, FINTRAC-regulated businesses such as banks must report material discrepancies between your filed ISC information and what their own client checks turn up — so a mismatch between what you told your bank and what you told Corporations Canada can surface on its own.

## How do you respond to the inquiry in 30 days?

Respond before the deadline with one of two packages, depending on your situation:

**If your corporation has ISCs** (or should have been reporting some all along):

1. **Rebuild the register first.** Work out who actually meets the 25% or control-in-fact tests, looking through any holding companies to real individuals. For each ISC you need their full legal name, date of birth, residential address (and optionally an address for service), countries of citizenship and tax residence, the date they became an ISC, and a description of their significant control. Only the name, dates, description of control, and address for service are made public — date of birth, citizenship, and tax residency [are not published](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/corporations-canada/en/individuals-significant-control/individuals-significant-control-file-your-information).
2. **File the updated information** through Corporations Canada's Online Filing Centre ("View/change information on individuals with significant control"). The update itself is free; ISC information is otherwise filed together with your [$12 federal annual return](/articles/How-to-File-Your-Annual-Return-Federal-Canada).
3. **Keep the corrected register in your minute book** with the date of the update and the steps you took. Correcting a past "no ISC" filing is routine — filing late is far better than leaving a filing you know is wrong.

**If your corporation truly has no ISCs**, respond with the supporting documentation the notice asks for, which may include:

- a copy of your ISC register showing the "no ISC" determination and the required summary of steps taken;
- a written summary of those steps (who was asked, what was reviewed, when);
- your shareholder list showing how ownership is spread.

Either way, respond through the channel the notice specifies, keep a dated copy of everything you send, and don't let the deadline slip while you perfect the paperwork. If your ownership structure involves trusts, joint control, or a possible control-in-fact question, have a corporate lawyer review your analysis — the "control in fact" test is fact-specific, and an inquiry response is the wrong place to guess.

To be clear about what CRS is and isn't here: we are a registry filing service, not Corporations Canada, and nobody can make an inquiry "go away" — only a complete, accurate response closes it. What we can do is get your annual return and ISC information filed accurately and fast, and build you a minute book in which the ISC register actually holds up.

## What happens if you ignore it?

The consequences escalate, and they're the government's own list, not scare copy. A corporation that doesn't respond may be treated as in default, and Corporations Canada's stated measures include:

- **Refusing a Certificate of Compliance** — the document lenders, landlords, and purchasers routinely demand in financing and sale transactions. A refused certificate can stall a deal at the worst possible moment.
- **Applying to court for a compliance order** against the corporation.
- **Taking steps toward administrative dissolution.** Corporations Canada can dissolve corporations that fail to file ISC information — the corporate equivalent of being struck from the register, with frozen bank accounts and a revival filing to undo it.
- **Prosecution.** Failing to file ISC information is an offence; on summary conviction a corporation faces a fine of up to $100,000. Under the CBCA, directors, officers, and shareholders who *knowingly* contravene the ISC rules or file false or misleading information face fines of up to $1,000,000, imprisonment for up to five years, or both.

The knowing-contravention penalties are reserved for deliberate conduct — an honest corporation that responds late or imperfectly is not facing five years in prison. But the Certificate of Compliance refusal and the dissolution track apply to simple non-response, which is why the 30-day window matters.

## How do you make sure you never get another one?

Run the "reasonable steps" routine the CBCA already expects, and document it. At minimum, **once every year** — most corporations fold this into their annual return — send a written information request to:

- every ISC on your register, asking them to confirm or update their information;
- all shareholders, asking whether they've become an ISC or know of one;
- anyone else the corporation has reasonable grounds to believe may have relevant knowledge.

Corporations Canada publishes a [request-for-information template](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/corporations-canada/en/individuals-significant-control) for exactly this. Keep the requests and the responses with the register, record "steps taken" and the date, update the register within 15 days whenever you learn of a change, and file the update. A register that shows an annual request cycle is precisely the supporting documentation a future inquiry asks for — you'd already have the response sitting in your minute book.

That's the real fix: the ISC register is one of the statutory registers that [belongs in your corporate minute book](/guides/what-is-a-corporate-minute-book-canada), next to your registers of directors and shareholders. If your corporation doesn't have a minute book — or has one that hasn't been touched since incorporation — CRS builds complete, compliant [digital minute books](/minute-books) including the ISC register, from {{price:minute-book-young-crs}} + GST built for you. And since ISC information is confirmed with every federal annual return, the simplest guardrail is making sure that return is actually filed each year: CRS files [federal annual returns](/order/annual-return?src=article-corporations-canada-isc-inquiry) with updated ISC information for {{price:annual-return}} all-in + tax, within 1 business day.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the ISC inquiry email from Corporations Canada legitimate?

Corporations Canada has been issuing official ISC inquiries by email since the fall of 2026, so a real inquiry is entirely plausible — but verify before you click. Check that the sender is a government address and that links point to ised-isde.canada.ca or canada.ca, or respond through the Online Filing Centre directly. If in doubt, contact Corporations Canada through its published channels rather than the email.

### What does "individuals with significant control" actually mean?

An ISC is an individual who owns or controls 25% or more of a corporation's voting shares, 25% or more of its shares by fair market value, or who has control in fact over the corporation — alone, jointly, or through a chain of holding companies. Every CBCA corporation must keep an ISC register and file the information with Corporations Canada, where part of it is publicly searchable.

### What happens if I miss the 30-day deadline to respond?

The corporation may be considered in default. Corporations Canada's stated measures include refusing a Certificate of Compliance, seeking a court compliance order, and taking steps toward administrative dissolution — and non-filing is an offence carrying a fine of up to $100,000 for the corporation. Respond late rather than never, and fix the underlying filing at the same time.

### My corporation filed "no ISC" — was that wrong?

Not necessarily. A "no ISC" filing is correct where no individual meets the 25% or control-in-fact tests — for example, several unrelated shareholders each under 25%. But the register must document the steps taken to reach that conclusion, and that summary is what an inquiry asks you to produce. If your corporation is owned through a holding company, look again: the individual controlling the holdco is usually an ISC of your corporation too.
